Vignette:
# Priya's Story

Priya was thirty years old when she first scheduled a therapy appointment, though the tremor in her voice when she called suggested someone far younger—someone still caught in an older terror. She had been married to Arun for five years, worked as a software engineer at a mid-sized tech firm in the suburbs, and had spent the better part of two decades convincing herself that what happened when she was nine years old no longer mattered. The past few months had made that conviction impossible to maintain.

The trauma itself had no single moment of clarity in Priya's mind, which troubled her deeply. Her father, who had struggled with alcohol for years, had cornered her in the kitchen one afternoon while her mother was at work. What followed was a sustained episode of physical violence—slaps, a hand gripped around her wrist, the smell of whiskey and sweat overwhelming her as he shouted accusations about her grades. But when Priya tried to recall the sequence now, the images would not arrange themselves in order. Sometimes she remembered his hand first; sometimes the taste of blood came before the sound of his voice. The confusion itself had become a secondary wound, as if the trauma had fractured not just her sense of safety but her ability to even narrate what had been done to her. When she tried to push through the confusion and hold the full memory in mind, the emotional flood would arrive so suddenly that she would have to stop, to push the whole thing away again, to retreat into the safer blankness of not remembering.

The triggers had accumulated quietly at first. A particular brand of cologne at the grocery store—something with a sharp, alcoholic top note—would send her into a state of hypervigilance that could last hours. The taste of iron, or certain spices her mother used in cooking, would bring back the metallic taste of that afternoon. And the smell of sweat, especially in warm weather or during exercise, would make her skin crawl with a dread she could not articulate. Arun had noticed her flinching away from him after the gym, and when he'd tried to hold her one evening, the combination of his warmth and the salt-smell of his skin had caused her to pull away so forcefully that she'd nearly fallen.

The hypervigilance had metastasized into her home life in ways that embarrassed her. She checked the locks on the front and back doors multiple times each night—often five, six, sometimes ten times before she could even attempt sleep. The checking had become ritualistic, compulsive, a way of manufacturing the certainty that danger could not breach the threshold. Yet the certainty never lasted. Within minutes of returning to bed, the doubt would creep back, and she would rise again to check. Arun had begun sleeping in the guest room. He loved her, he said, but the nightly checking, her sudden tensing at sounds he could not hear, her inability to relax even when they were locked inside with the alarm system armed—it was exhausting him.

Sleep itself had become a battleground. Her mind would race with scenarios: windows left slightly ajar, the back gate not quite latched, someone standing outside in the dark. Even on nights when she managed to fall asleep, she would wake at 2 or 3 a.m., heart pounding, certain that something had changed. She had taken to sleeping with her phone in one hand and her keys on the nightstand, though she could not explain why keys would be useful inside a locked bedroom.

At work, Priya had begun to notice the consequences. She was missing meetings because she had overslept after finally collapsing from exhaustion around dawn. Her code reviews had become sloppy—her mind would drift, or worse, a scent from the office kitchen would send her into a fugue state where she could not focus for an hour. Her manager had pulled her aside last month to ask if everything was okay. She had lied and said it was just stress, just a rough patch. What she could not say was that she felt unsafe in her own body, that the past had become a stalker that followed her into the present, that she could not trust her own mind to hold a coherent memory of the thing that had broken her.

It was Arun's suggestion that she finally call. He had found her at 3 a.m. checking the locks again, and something in his face—not anger, but a deep sadness—had made her realize that the life she was living was no longer a life at all. She was existing in a state of perpetual threat, and she did not know how to stop.
